title: Chapter 5 — Breakfast
paragraphs: I quickly followed suit and went down to the bar room, greeting the grinning landlord very pleasantly. I bore him no grudge, though he had played more than a few pranks on me in the matter of my bedfellow.

However, a good laugh is a mighty good thing, and rather too scarce a good thing — more's the pity. So if any man, in his own proper person, provides material for a good joke to anybody, let him not hold back, but let him cheerfully allow himself to spend and be spent in that way. And the man who has anything bountifully laughable about him — be sure there is more in that man than you perhaps think.

The bar room was now full of the boarders who had been dropping in the night before, and whom I had not yet had a good look at. They were nearly all whalemen — chief mates, second mates, third mates, sea carpenters, sea coopers, sea blacksmiths, harpooners, and ship keepers; a brown and brawny company with bushy beards — an unshaven, shaggy set, all wearing monkey jackets for morning robes.

You could tell pretty plainly how long each one had been ashore. This young fellow's healthy cheek is the color of a sun-toasted pear, and would seem to smell almost as musky; he can't have been three days landed from his Indian voyage. The man next to him looks a few shades lighter; you might say there is a touch of satinwood in him. In the complexion of a third there still lingers a tropical tan, though slightly bleached by now; he, no doubt, has stayed whole weeks ashore. But who could show a cheek like Queequeg's? Barred with various tints, it seemed like the western slope of the Andes, showing in one array contrasting climates, zone by zone.
"Grub, ho!" the landlord now cried, flinging open a door, and in we went to breakfast.

They say that men who have seen the world become quite at ease in manner, quite self-possessed in company as a result. Not always, though: Ledyard, the great New England traveler, and Mungo Park, the Scottish one — of all men, they had the least assurance in the parlor. But perhaps merely crossing Siberia in a sledge drawn by dogs, as Ledyard did, or taking a long solitary walk on an empty stomach in the negro heart of Africa, which was the sum of poor Mungo's achievements — this kind of travel, I say, may not be the very best way of acquiring a high social polish. Still, for the most part, that sort of polish is to be had anywhere.

These reflections are prompted just here by the fact that after we were all seated at the table, and I was preparing to hear some good stories about whaling, to my no small surprise nearly every man kept a profound silence. And not only that, but they looked embarrassed. Yes, here was a set of sea dogs, many of whom had, without the slightest bashfulness, boarded great whales on the high seas — entire strangers to them — and dueled them dead without blinking; and yet here they sat at a social breakfast table — all of the same calling, all of kindred tastes — looking around at each other as sheepishly as though they had never been out of sight of some sheepfold among the Green Mountains. A curious sight — these bashful bears, these timid warrior whalemen!

But Queequeg sat among them — at the head of the table, as it happened — cool as an icicle. To be sure, I can't say much for his breeding. His greatest admirer couldn't have heartily justified his bringing the harpoon to breakfast and using it without ceremony — reaching across the table with it, endangering many heads, and hooking the beefsteaks toward himself. But that he certainly did very coolly, and everyone knows that in most people's estimation, to do anything coolly is to do it genteelly.

We won't dwell on all of Queequeg's peculiarities here — how he avoided coffee and hot rolls and devoted his full attention to beefsteaks, done rare. Enough to say that after breakfast he withdrew like the others to the public room, lit his tomahawk-pipe, and sat there quietly digesting and smoking with his inseparable hat on, while I headed out for a walk.
